coverage_limits: The anonymous OpenAlex budget for this network ran out early in the run, so the citing-works pass for Hohenstein et al. and all later OpenAlex searches were replaced by Semantic Scholar citation lists; the Semantic Scholar search endpoint returned HTTP 429 for most of 18 keyword queries, so keyword coverage there is thin. ACM DL, Springer and SSRN pages blocked scripted access, so five records rest on Crossref metadata without abstracts (Bauer 2025, Ren 2026, Chen/Brandimarte/Susarla 2024, de Rooij and Biskjaer ECCE 2026, Anderson et al. CHI EA 2024) and their designs are unconfirmed. Random assignment could not be confirmed for many experiments, which are marked experiment_assignment_unclear. Non-English databases (for example CNKI) were not searched, and EFL writing studies whose only outcome is within-text lexical diversity or writing quality were mostly left out. The University of Amsterdam thesis is known only from a search snippet (the page now returns 404).

candidates.title: How LLMs Distort Our Written Language
candidates.task: argumentative essay (does money lead to happiness?)
candidates.evidence: 100 participants were randomly assigned to write without an LLM (n=45) or with an embedded gpt-4o-mini assistant (n=55). Heavy LLM use raised the share of neutral-stance essays by about 70 percent, and heavy-use essays formed a tight cluster in embedding space while unassisted essays spread out; the paper adds LLM-revision and peer-review analyses.

candidates.title: Incentives shape how humans co-create with generative AI
candidates.task: short story writing (250-350 words)
candidates.evidence: 200 Prolific participants were block-randomized in a 2x2 design: write alone or with a GPT-5-mini assistant, and be paid for quality or for originality relative to peers. Collective diversity was measured with embedding and n-gram similarity; AI-assisted stories were more similar than human-only stories at submission, and originality pay reduced the gap.

candidates.title: Human Thinking under Plural LLM Assistance: Mathematical Problem Solving and Open-Ended Writing
candidates.task: argumentative and creative essays
candidates.evidence: Between-subjects writing experiment with no LLM, one generalist assistant, or a pair of role-specialized assistants; 247 of 419 recruits gave usable essays (562 people across the paper's two experiments). LLM help raised rubric-rated quality, including originality, and the specialized pair kept more idea diversity (pairwise similarity of extracted key points) than the single assistant; random assignment to conditions is not explicit in the text read.

candidates.title: Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration
candidates.task: 1,000-word short story writing
candidates.evidence: 285 students wrote a story without AI on day 1, then were randomly assigned on day 2 to one of three ChatGPT 3.5 collaboration models (human confirmation, human creativity, copilot). Stories were rated for quality, originality and interestingness; more AI involvement lowered the aggregate diversity of stories and genres across participants.

candidates.title: Effects of Varying LLM Access on Essay Writing Behavior
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 21st Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2026), pp. 685-701
candidates.task: short essay writing by college students
candidates.evidence: 24 college students were randomly assigned to write a short essay with no LLM, limited LLM access (3 prompts, 100-word replies) or unlimited access. Quality did not differ, but the unlimited group's essays were more similar to LLM output and its members reported less creative expression.

candidates.title: Can You Make It Sound Like You? Post-Editing LLM-Generated Text for Personal Style
candidates.authors: Baumler, Bao, Nghiem, Yang, Carpuat, Daumé
candidates.task: post-editing LLM drafts for personal-style writing tasks
candidates.evidence: Pre-registered online study (n=81): participants post-edited LLM drafts and also wrote unassisted control texts. Embedding-based style measures show post-edited text stays closer to LLM style than to the writer's own style and has lower stylistic diversity than unassisted human text.

candidates.title: Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI
candidates.task: analytical essay after reading on an unfamiliar topic
candidates.evidence: Undergraduates (211 in session one, 204 in both sessions) were randomized by lab and seat to write an analytical essay with or without generative AI, then wrote unaided one week later. Within-group pairwise cosine similarity of essays showed a near-zero, insignificant effect, so no homogenization; co-authored by the atlas owner (Reyes).

candidates.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
candidates.task: SAT-style essay writing over four sessions
candidates.evidence: 54 participants wrote essays in three sessions as LLM, search-engine or brain-only groups, and 18 returned for a fourth session with conditions switched (LLM-to-brain, brain-to-LLM). NLP analysis found within-group homogeneity of named entities, n-grams and topics; the fourth session removes AI but reports mainly neural and recall outcomes, and how groups were formed is not stated in the abstract.

candidates.title: Biased AI writing assistants shift users’ attitudes on societal issues
candidates.authors: Williams-Ceci, Jakesch, Bhat, Kadoma, Zalmanson, Naaman
other_versions: doi 10.31234/osf.io/mhjn6 (PsyArXiv 2024, titled Bias in AI Autocomplete Suggestions Leads to Attitude Shift on Societal Issues)
candidates.task: writing about societal issues with biased autocomplete suggestions
candidates.evidence: Two preregistered experiments (N=2,582) exposed people writing about societal issues to an AI assistant that gave biased autocomplete suggestions. Post-task attitudes converged toward the AI's position, more than with the same content shown as static text, and bias warnings did not remove the effect; the abstract does not state the assignment procedure.

candidates.title: Co-Writing with Opinionated Language Models Affects Users' Views
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23)
candidates.task: post on whether social media is good for society
candidates.evidence: 1,506 participants were randomly assigned to write with no assistant or with a GPT-3 assistant configured to argue that social media is good or bad for society. Opinions expressed in the posts (judged by 500 raters) and later survey attitudes shifted toward the assistant's stance.

candidates.title: AI Writing Assistants Influence Topic Choice in Self-Presentation
candidates.venue: Extended Abstracts of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 1-6
candidates.task: written self-introduction with sentence-completion suggestions
candidates.evidence: Online experiment (N=200) in which people wrote self-introductions with suggestions from a model tuned to favor interest, work or hospitality topics. The model's topic preference shifted the topics people wrote about; design details come from the NSF PAR abstract seen in search results, since Crossref has no abstract.

candidates.title: When Stereotypes GTG: The Impact of Predictive Text Suggestions on Gender Bias in Human-AI Co-Writing
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 1-44
candidates.task: completing story openings with single-word predictive text
candidates.evidence: 414 Prolific participants completed story openings with no suggestions or with LM predictive text that was pro- or anti-stereotypical. Anti-stereotypical suggestions sometimes raised anti-stereotypical stories but pro-stereotypical stories still dominated; the outcome is stereotype content, not a creativity or diversity index, and is listed as an LM-suggestion content-shift study.

candidates.title: Measuring and Mitigating Persona Distortions from AI Writing Assistance
candidates.task: political opinion paragraphs written with and without AI
candidates.evidence: In three experiments, 2,939 writers wrote political opinion paragraphs with and without AI assistance (a within-writer comparison) and 11,091 readers rated them on 29 dimensions. AI-assisted paragraphs read as more opinionated, competent and privileged, and reader ratings of AI-assisted paragraphs were more alike than ratings of human-written ones.

candidates.title: "Hi Alex" or "Dear Dr. Morgan"?: Exploring How AI-suggested Politeness Strategies Influence Email Writing and Social Perception Among Native and Non-native Speakers
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 10(6), pp. 1-33
candidates.task: email writing with AI suggestions
candidates.evidence: Within-subject online study (N=52) varying the politeness strategy in AI email suggestions. Writers mirrored the suggested strategy in their own emails, and non-native English speakers shifted more than native speakers.

candidates.title: AI-Generated Email Drafts Shift Culturally Distinctive Communication Styles in Professional Email
candidates.task: workplace emails in the writer's native language
candidates.evidence: Preregistered study with 175 employed adults (86 Japanese, 89 American) who wrote workplace emails without AI and then with a low-context and a high-context AI draft, in counterbalanced order. AI drafts pulled emails toward the draft's cultural style, most when the draft clashed with the writer's culture.

candidates.title: Artificial intelligence in communication impacts language and social relationships
candidates.task: text conversations with algorithmic reply suggestions
candidates.evidence: Two randomized experiments on smart-reply suggestions in conversations. Suggestions raised the use of positive emotional language and changed how partners rated each other; borderline because there is no creativity or diversity index, and sample size is not in the abstract.

candidates.title: Who wrote this? How smart replies impact language and agency in the workplace
candidates.task: workplace messages with smart replies
candidates.evidence: Crowdsourced mixed-methods experiment on smart replies; machine suggestions changed the content people authored. Borderline: the outcome is content and agency rather than creativity or diversity, and the abstract does not say whether a generative model produced the replies.

candidates.title: The Unexpected Effects of Google Smart Compose on Open-Ended Writing Tasks
candidates.venue: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED 2024), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, pp. 468-481
candidates.task: 25-minute open-ended response (hard work or luck?)
candidates.evidence: 119 participants wrote with a plain word processor or with Google Smart Compose. The university news release reports no significant quantitative or qualitative effect on the writing; abstract not retrieved, so content or similarity measures are unconfirmed.

candidates.title: Exploring the Impact of AI Value Alignment in Collaborative Ideation: Effects on Perception, Ownership, and Output
candidates.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '24), pp. 1-11
candidates.task: brainstorming practical solutions with AI agents
candidates.evidence: 180 participants brainstormed solutions with AI agents holding different values. Ideas took on the agent's values and ownership changed, while self-rated idea quality did not differ; an AI-variant comparison with no stated no-AI arm.

candidates.title: Reactive Writers: How Co-Writing with AI Changes How We Engage with Ideas
candidates.authors: Bhat, Aubin Le Quéré, Naaman, Jakesch
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 1-21
candidates.task: AI co-writing sessions on opinion topics
candidates.evidence: Interviews with 19 people plus a trace analysis of 1,291 AI co-writing sessions. Writers often read suggestions before finishing their own ideation, so suggested ideas and opinions seeded what they wrote; this explains opinion shifts but adds no new randomized comparison.

candidates.title: Overreliance in Writing Tasks: Exploring Similarity-Based Measures of AI Influence on Writing and Proposing a Reflective Writing Interface Intervention
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '26), pp. 5941-5958
candidates.task: analysis and synthesis writing tasks
candidates.evidence: 47 participants did writing tasks with or without AI assistance, and the authors measured textual overlap between AI suggestions and the final text. AI assistance went with reuse of suggestion text; a small think-aloud study (n=4) tested a reflective interface.

candidates.title: Hybrid Human–AI Societies Balance Creativity and Diversity
other_versions: arXiv 2502.17962 (The Dynamics of Collective Creativity in Human-AI Hybrid Societies; CogSci 2025)
candidates.task: story selection, modification and transmission in social networks
candidates.evidence: Network experiments with 1,363 human participants and 7,865 AI bots who selected, modified and passed on stories in human-only, AI-only or hybrid networks. Raters scored creativity and collective diversity was tracked; hybrid networks kept the highest diversity, and humans in hybrid networks became more diverse than in human-only networks.

candidates.title: Humans Introduce, Models Elaborate: Asymmetric Narrative Agency in Human-LLM Co-Writing
candidates.task: turn-based collaborative storytelling
candidates.evidence: Matched human-human, human-LLM and LLM-LLM storytelling conditions scored with turn-level semantic novelty and influence measures. Humans added more novel, lasting material while LLMs elaborated; the full text reports about 205 human participants, but per-condition counts and assignment were unclear.

candidates.title: Is ChatGPT detrimental to innovation? A field experiment among university students
candidates.venue: Review of Economics and Political Science 11(4), 264-282
candidates.task: graded essays over a month, then a lab innovation game without AI
candidates.evidence: About 100 senior students in Egypt wrote three graded essays over a month, the treatment group with ChatGPT and the control without. Both groups then played a lab innovation game without AI, and the ChatGPT group scored 0.6-0.72 SD lower on innovation.

candidates.title: Is Chatgpt a menace for creative writing ability? An experiment
candidates.task: creative writing essays by university students
candidates.evidence: 600 students from 10 universities formed a control group and an experimental group that used ChatGPT in creative writing. Essays were scored for originality, content presentation, accuracy and elaboration, and ChatGPT use was linked to lower scores; assignment and whether the scored essays were written without ChatGPT are unclear from the abstract.

candidates.title: ChatGPT-3.5 as writing assistance in students’ essays
candidates.task: student essays
candidates.evidence: 18 students wrote essays, 9 with ChatGPT-3 and 9 without. Grades did not improve with ChatGPT, and content similarity among essays (Jaccard index, 0 to 0.054) was low across the sample.

candidates.title: Augmenting Minds or Automating Skills: The Differential Role of Human Capital in Generative AI's Impact on Creative Tasks
candidates.task: flash fiction writing and song composition
candidates.evidence: Two randomized controlled experiments, in flash fiction writing and song composition, compare creative output with and without generative AI across levels of human capital. AI help favored general cognitive ability and education over domain expertise; sample sizes are not in the abstract.

candidates.title: Human direction drives creativity with large language models
candidates.task: brainstorming and writing with ChatGPT or Gemini
candidates.evidence: Two controlled experiments with ChatGPT (N=234, N=205), a preregistered replication with Gemini (N=157) and 6,290 naturalistic chats score how much people direct rather than delegate creative work. More direction predicted more original output and lower semantic similarity across people; direction is measured, not assigned.

candidates.title: Evaluating Creativity Support Tools via Homogenization Analysis
candidates.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '24), pp. 1-7
candidates.task: ideation with ChatGPT versus another creativity support tool
candidates.evidence: Extended abstract proposing homogenization analysis (similarity of ideas across users) to evaluate creativity support tools such as ChatGPT. Abstract not retrieved; a search summary ties it to the authors' already-collected C&C 2024 user study, so it may reuse those data.

candidates.title: Human vs. AI Partner: Who Inspires Greater Creativity in Collaborative Story Writing?
candidates.venue: Master's thesis, University of Amsterdam (Brain and Cognition programme), presentation listing
candidates.task: story writing alone, with a human partner, and with GPT-5.1
candidates.evidence: 40 participants (20 pairs) wrote stories alone, with a human partner and with GPT-5.1; expert ratings and automated metrics scored diversity, novelty, surprise and complexity. Human-human stories were more semantically diverse and surprising than human-AI stories; known only from a search snippet of the event page, which now returns 404.

candidates.title: Examining Human-AI Collaboration for Co-Writing Constructive Comments Online
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 9(7), Article 410 (CSCW 2025)
candidates.task: constructive comments on Islamophobia and homophobia threads
candidates.evidence: Controlled experiments with 600 Indian and US participants; in the writing experiment 104 people (52 Indian, 52 US) were randomly assigned to write comments alone or with an LLM. Similarity among comments (cosine, semantic) was about the same in both groups, while lexical diversity (distinct-2, type-token ratio) was higher with the LLM.

candidates.title: Generative AI Makes Creative Output More Homogeneous
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 European Conference on Cognitive Ergonomics (ECCE 2026), pp. 198-201
candidates.evidence: Four-page ECCE paper by the authors of the already-collected homogenisation meta-analysis (Behaviour & Information Technology 2026). Abstract not retrieved; title and authors suggest a short version of that synthesis, so treat it as a possible other version.

candidates.title: Does ChatGPT Increase Language Homogenization?
candidates.venue: KI in Medien, Kommunikation und Marketing (Springer), pp. 11-31
candidates.evidence: Book chapter whose title asks whether ChatGPT homogenizes language. Abstract and design could not be retrieved (the Springer page needs a login); listed for recall only.

candidates.title: Human-AI Interaction in L2 Writing Support: Homogenization in LLM Revisions of Learner Errors
candidates.venue: Journal of Humanities, Arts and Social Science 10(7), 747-756
candidates.task: LLM revision of second-language learner errors
candidates.evidence: Title indicates an analysis of homogenization when LLMs revise second-language learners' errors. Crossref has no abstract, so the design (possibly LLM revisions of learner texts with no participants) is unconfirmed.

candidates.title: Does Increasing Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Boost Creativity? Assessing AI-Augmented Creativity with Large Language Models
candidates.evidence: SSRN paper found among works citing the opinionated-LM and predictive-text studies; the title points to a test of creativity under increasing reliance on LLMs. The SSRN page returned 403 and Crossref has no abstract, so design and outcomes are unconfirmed.

candidates.title: Introducing AI to an online petition platform changed outputs but not outcomes
candidates.task: petitions on Change.org before and after a write-with-AI tool
candidates.evidence: Natural experiment: difference-in-differences on 1.5 million Change.org petitions around the launch of an in-platform write-with-AI tool, confirmed with repeat writers. AI access changed lexical features and raised petition homogeneity but did not improve petition outcomes.

candidates.title: The Syntactic Exoskeleton: How Generative AI Homogenizes the Structure of Arabic-L1 English Academic Writing
candidates.task: English academic essays by Arabic-L1 undergraduates
candidates.evidence: Corpus comparison of 423 essays: unassisted exam essays (n=339) versus GenAI-mediated assignments (n=84). GenAI-mediated texts had much lower sentence-length variance and lost L1 clause-chaining patterns; the groups differ by task, not by assignment.

candidates.title: Can We Still Trace L1 Signals? Investigating the Resilience of Native Language Signals in the LLM Era
candidates.task: native-language identification on academic abstracts
candidates.evidence: Native-language identification on arXiv and ACL abstracts from eight L1 groups across pre-neural, pre-LLM and post-LLM periods, plus an LLM rewriting test. Identification accuracy fell over time, mostly before LLMs, and LLM rewriting cut it further, a sign of homogenizing academic English.

candidates.title: AI-Associated Lexical Shifts Across 34 Languages: Cross-Lingual Convergence and Diachronic Uptake in News Writing
candidates.task: news writing in 34 languages
candidates.evidence: Finds AI-overused words per language by comparing GPT-4.1 continuations with human news text, then tracks them in news writing. Similar concepts are overused across languages, and their use in news rose in 26 of 34 languages after ChatGPT's release.

candidates.title: What Are LLMs Doing to Scientific Communication? Measuring Changes in Writing Practices and Reading Experience
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the Fifteenth Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2026), pp. 1811-1830
candidates.task: NLP research papers (ACL Anthology 2020-2024)
candidates.evidence: Diachronic analysis of about 37,000 ACL Anthology papers plus 3,000 human passages and their LLM-improved versions. LLM-modified texts show lower lexical diversity and distinct syntax; 20 experts rated LLM-improved texts as clearer.

candidates.title: How Did Writing Change At CHI? Analyzing 44 Years of CHI Writing Before and After the Introduction of Large Language Models
candidates.task: CHI paper full texts, 1982-2026
candidates.evidence: Full texts of 14,262 CHI papers analyzed for readability, register, lexical diversity and LLM marker words. Prose did not homogenize and vocabulary grew more varied; word-level shifts began before LLMs, which sped them up.

candidates.title: From "Effects of X on Y" to "From X to Y": Evidence of Stylistic Convergence in Academic Titles after Mass LLM Adoption
candidates.task: academic paper titles, 2010-2026
candidates.evidence: Tracks the 'From X to Y' title pattern in 2,039,999 OpenAlex titles across twelve fields. Its share nearly doubled after 2023, mostly in fields with low prior use, which the author reads as convergence of disciplinary title styles.

candidates.title: Writing in Symbiosis: Mapping Human Creative Agency in the AI Era
candidates.task: longitudinal creative writing corpus
candidates.evidence: Large longitudinal creative-writing corpus spanning the pre- and post-LLM eras. Reports thematic convergence on AI topics alongside stylistic differentiation, with some authors moving toward AI style and others away.

candidates.title: The Lock-in Hypothesis: Stagnation by Algorithm
candidates.task: real-world GPT usage data and agent simulations
candidates.evidence: Agent-based LLM simulations plus real-world GPT usage data. Concept diversity in the usage data dropped and stayed lower after new GPT releases; the abstract does not separate user-written from model-written text.

candidates.title: Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization and Shared Language Technology: Evidence from Reddit
candidates.task: political comments on two cross-partisan Reddit forums, 2019-2025
candidates.evidence: 6 million Reddit comments: conservative users' prior diversification trend broke around late 2022 while progressive users' did not. The effect fades among long-active authors, so the author reads it as community-level convergence rather than individual AI adoption.

candidates.title: The Role of AI in Online Reviews
candidates.task: Trustpilot business reviews
candidates.evidence: Uses LLM supply shocks and verified versus unverified status in more than 13 million Trustpilot reviews. Unverified reviews turned more negative after shocks; embedding-based textual homogeneity was measured, but its effects were not significant (supplementary tables).

candidates.title: Converging Naming Styles, Persistent Network Locality: GitHub in the LLM Era
candidates.task: identifier naming in public GitHub repositories, 2015-2025
candidates.evidence: Public repositories in six programming languages coded on 27 naming-style features. Repositories with LLM-related commits lean toward already common patterns, and naming-style diversity fell in recent cohorts; code rather than prose, included for the convergence outcome.

candidates.title: One Tool, One Taste? How Vibe Coding Trades Collective Diversity for Individual Creativity
candidates.task: promotional websites built with a vibe-coding tool
candidates.evidence: 73 promotional websites built by graduate students with Lovable were compared through image embeddings. Sites concentrated in a few visual clusters despite an assignment that graded originality; there is no no-AI comparison group.

candidates.title: Do Large Language Models Always Tell The Same Stories?
candidates.task: stories for r/WritingPrompts prompts
candidates.evidence: Human and automatic narrative-similarity judgments for stories from 10 LLMs and from human r/WritingPrompts authors. LLM stories are more similar to each other than human stories are, and negative prompting or higher temperature did not fix this.

candidates.title: Narrative Flattening: How Post-Training Compresses Thematic, Affective, and Stylistic Variation in LLM Fiction
candidates.task: story continuations
candidates.evidence: Matched story continuations from four OLMo 32B checkpoints compared with human text from StoryStar, a prompt-guided corpus and The New Yorker. Post-training shrank thematic, affective and stylistic variation across stories relative to human baselines.

candidates.title: Novels generated by language models show compressed formal variation
candidates.task: full-length novels
candidates.evidence: Compares 80 novels generated by GPT-5.5 Thinking and Qwen3-14B with 205 nineteenth-century and 65 contemporary human novels on lexical, sentence and readability measures. Repeated generations vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels do.

candidates.title: Where Models Converge and Humans Diverge: A Coverage Framework for Distributional Pluralism in Open-Ended Generation
candidates.task: fan fiction, narratives and ideation responses
candidates.evidence: Proposes coverage metrics that use the distribution of human writing on a topic to measure the breadth of LLM output. Across ideation and narrative tasks, LLM content is plausible but concentrated near the center of the human response space.

candidates.title: LLMs Exhibit Significantly Lower Uncertainty in Creative Writing Than Professional Writers
candidates.task: story continuations
candidates.evidence: Information-theoretic comparison of human-authored stories with continuations from 28 LLMs. Human writing shows consistently higher uncertainty, and the gap is larger for instruction-tuned and reasoning models.

candidates.title: Echoes in AI: Quantifying lack of plot diversity in LLM outputs
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(35), e2504966122
candidates.task: short story generation
candidates.evidence: Introduces the Sui Generis score for how often plot elements recur across generations. GPT-4 and LLaMA-3 stories echo plot elements across generations and models, while plots of the original human-written stories are rarely recreated.

candidates.title: Large language models, social demography, and hegemony: comparing authorship in human and synthetic text
candidates.authors: Alvero, Lee, Regla-Vargas, Kizilcec, Joachims, Antonio
candidates.task: college admissions essays
candidates.evidence: Compares style features of over 150,000 admissions essays with more than 25,000 GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 essays written to the same prompts. Human essays vary more on individual style features, and AI essays most resemble those of more privileged male applicants.

candidates.title: Poor Alignment and Steerability of Large Language Models: Evidence from College Admission Essays
candidates.task: college admissions essays
candidates.evidence: Compares lexical and sentence variation in essays by 30,000 applicants with LLM essays prompted with the question alone or with applicant demographics. Synthetic essays are distinct from human ones, demographic prompting does not align them, and the two synthetic sets are more similar to each other than to human text.

candidates.title: Linguistic and Embedding-Based Profiling of Texts generated by Humans and Large Language Models
candidates.venue: Proceedings of EMNLP 2025 (per arXiv journal reference)
candidates.task: texts from 8 domains
candidates.evidence: Profiles human and machine texts from 8 domains and 11 LLMs on morphological, syntactic and semantic features plus style embeddings. Human texts show more semantic diversity and more feature variation, and newer models produce similarly variable text.

candidates.title: Do Large Language Models Produce Texts With “Human‐Like” Lexical Diversity? Evidence From Four ChatGPT Models
candidates.task: argumentative essays
candidates.evidence: Six lexical diversity dimensions compared between essays from four ChatGPT models and essays by 240 L1 and L2 English writers. ChatGPT texts differed from human texts on every dimension and newer models were least human-like; this is within-text diversity, not across-writer homogeneity.

candidates.title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
candidates.task: argumentative student essays
candidates.evidence: Teachers rated human-written and ChatGPT-generated argumentative essays and the authors compared linguistic features. ChatGPT essays were rated higher and, per the preprint abstract, showed greater lexical diversity and fewer discourse markers; context on within-text diversity only.

candidates.title: Voice Under Revision: Large Language Models and the Normalization of Personal Narrative
candidates.task: LLM rewriting of personal narratives
candidates.evidence: 300 human personal narratives were rewritten by three frontier LLMs under three prompts and compared on 13 stylometric markers. Rewrites converged in feature space and became harder to match to their sources, even with voice-preserving prompts; no person used the AI.

candidates.title: The Assistant Erased You: Measuring Loss of Authorship Signals in AI-Mediated Communication
candidates.task: AI rewriting of blogs, workplace email and news
candidates.evidence: Rewrites texts from three pre-AI corpora with an AI assistant and measures the drop in authorship attribution. Heavy rewriting cut attribution accuracy by up to 66.5 points and produced stylistic convergence across authors.

candidates.title: The Cost of Perfect English: Pragmatic Flattening and the Erasure of Authorial Voice in L2 Writing Supported by GenAI
candidates.task: LLM polishing of Chinese students' argumentative essays (ICNALE)
candidates.evidence: Essays by Chinese B2-level students were polished by four LLMs and compared with the originals. Models removed dialogic engagement markers and reshaped stance, pulling texts toward an Anglo-American norm; no person used the AI.

candidates.title: Does AI Homogenize Student Thinking? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Structural Convergence in AI-Augmented Essays
candidates.task: student essays augmented by an LLM (AIDE corpus)
candidates.evidence: 1,375 human essays from the AIDE corpus were augmented by GPT-5-mini under three prompt strategies and compared with human-only and AI-only essays (6,875 essays in all). Augmentation raised quality and cut variance in cohesion structure by 70-78 percent; no students used the AI, so human-AI writing is simulated.

candidates.title: Large language models are homogeneously creative
other_versions: arXiv 2501.19361 (We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs; already collected)
candidates.task: standardized creativity tasks
candidates.evidence: Published version of an already-collected arXiv paper. Creative responses from many humans and many LLMs on standardized tasks show that LLM responses resemble each other far more than human responses do, after controls.

candidates.title: The shrinking landscape of linguistic diversity in the age of large language models
candidates.task: seven text datasets (news, papers, essays, posts, speeches)
candidates.evidence: Already collected; listed to give the Nature Human Behaviour version. Three studies over seven datasets and more than 880,000 texts link LLM writing assistance to lower linguistic diversity, and LLM rewriting cut writing-complexity variance by 21-50 percent.
